div.head: II Atr 9.2
div.ab: Gyf hwa to deadan tyme — buton he yruenoman hæbbe, ðe hit clænsie —, geswutelie mid gewitnysse, gif he mæge, þæt he riht cenne, se ðe hit tyme; ⁊ clænsnige hine sylfne mid ðam. Ðonne bið se deada besmiten, buton he frind hæbbe, ðe hine mid rihte clænsnian, swa he sylf scolde, gif he mehte oðð liues wære.

Si mortuum hominem aduocet — si non habeat heredes, qui purget eum —, manifestet hoc cum testibus, si possit, quod recte aduocet; ac per id se purget. Tunc erit mortuus in culpa, nisi amicos habeat, qui eum mundificent, sicut idem faceret, si posset ac uiueret.

Gyf hwa to deadan tyme—buton he yruenoman hæbbe ðe hit clænsie—geswutelie mid gewitnysse, gif he mæge, þæt he riht cenne se ðe hit tyme ⁊ clænsnige hine sylfne mid ðam. Ðonne bið se deada besmiten, buton he frind hæbbe ðe hine mid rihte clænsnian, swa he sylf scolde, gif he mehte oðð liues wære.

Wenn jemand die Gewähr auf einen Verstorbenen zieht — ausser wenn dieser einen Erbnehmer hat, der das [im Anefang Gefasste von Schuld] rein erweisen will —, beweise er, wer es schiebt, durch Zeugenschaft, wenn er kann, dass er richtig [Gewähr] angiebt, und reinige hiermit sich selbst. Dann ist jener Verstorbene [schuld]befleckt, es sei denn, er hat Freunde, die ihn gesetzmässig als rein erweisen, so wie er selbst, wenn er könnte oder am Leben wäre, [es thun] müsste.

If anyone vouches a dead man to warranty — unless he has an heir who will clear [the attached item of guilt] —, let him who vouches it prove by witness, if he can, that he is declaring [the warranty] correctly, and so clear himself. Then the dead man is tainted [with guilt], unless he has friends who will clear him lawfully, as he himself would have had to, if he could or were alive.

If anyone vouches a dead person to warranty—unless he have an heir who can answer the charge—he who vouches him to warranty shall show by means of witnesses, if he can, that he is acting justly, and by means of them shall clear himself. Then the dead man will be held guilty, unless he have friends who will clear him according to the law, as he himself would have been obliged to do, had he been able or had he been alive.

note.seg: Vgl. Gl Anefang 12. 22. a. b.; Tote 2—4. Der Erbe, der nicht reinigen will, gibt die Sache heraus, aber ohne Diebstahlbusse; Rauch 35
Cf. Gl Anefang 12. 22. a. b.; Tote 2—4. The heir who is unwilling to clear [it] gives up the thing, but without compensation for theft; Rauch 35

Nicht den Toten (wie im folgenden Satze⁵ und 9, 3), den Q versteht, reinigt hier der Erbnehmer, sondern durch Ureigenerklärung oder Gewährzug den angeschlagenen Gegenstand als von jenem rechtmässig besessen

What the heir clears here is not the dead man (as in the following sentence⁵ and 9, 3), as Q understands it, but the attached object, as having been lawfully possessed by the deceased, by a declaration of original ownership or by vouching to warranty
Vouching to warranty requires witnesses; above 9, 1²

Der Tote kann gereinigt werden nicht bloss durch jenes Erbnehmers Erklärung, sondern auch laut Ine 53, 1 durch den Beweis kraft Eides der Sippe (s. d. 21), er habe das Angeschlagene nie besessen. Sonst hätte ein Besitzer von Diebstahl leicht der Strafe entschlüpfen können, indem er auf einen Toten ohne Erbnehmer und Sippe Gewähr zog

The dead man can be cleared not only by that heir’s declaration, but also, according to Ine 53, 1, by proof on the oath of the kindred (see that word 21) that he never possessed the attached thing. Otherwise a possessor of stolen goods could easily have escaped punishment by vouching to warranty a dead man without heir or kindred

Cf. In. 53 f.; Ancient Laws and Institutes of Wales, p. 209 f. One clause in a London Municipal collection of the time of John provides for the taking of an oath at the tomb of a dead man regarding the testimony he would have borne if alive, and ‘in Manx law until 1609 when a debtor died and no writings remained to prove his debt, the creditor might come to the dead man’s grave,…and, with his face toward Heaven and with a Bible on his breast, protest before God and by that book that the dead man owed him the money, and the executors were bound to pay’ (see M. Bateson in E.H.R., 1902, p. 488 f.).
